client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed thinking about my final exams coming up next month. After barely passing chemistry last semester, I'm terrified I'm going to fail it again, and the stress is making it hard to focus on any of my other classes either. I'm not sure talking about it will help when I just need to study more, but I don't know how to stop panicking about it.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying a heavy weight of worry about your exams, especially chemistry, and that past experience is making it feel even more daunting. When our minds get caught in that cycle of panic, it can be tough to see any way out—but let's explore how we might shift that perspective together.  

I hear the fear in your voice, along with a sense of exhaustion—like you're trying to push through but feeling stuck. What if we looked at what *did* work last semester, even just barely passing, as a starting point?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess barely passing last semester was something, but it doesn’t feel like much of a win. I still feel like I’m not good enough, and now the pressure is even worse because I can’t afford to fail again. I keep imagining the worst-case scenarios—like failing and disappointing everyone—and it’s paralyzing. I don’t know how to stop thinking like that.
therapist:
Your voice tightens when you talk about failing again—it’s clear how much this fear has taken hold. Those worst-case scenarios feel so real right now, but let’s pause and ask: What evidence do you have that *this* time will inevitably end in failure?  

The pressure you’re describing sounds crushing, but I wonder if we could untangle it together—starting with the thought that you’re "not good enough." Where does that story come from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I guess the "not good enough" thing comes from always comparing myself to others who seem to have it together. Like last week at work, my presentation didn't go perfectly and I just keep replaying every little mistake. It's exhausting, but I can't seem to stop feeling like I'm falling short.

I know logically that not every presentation is flawless, but in the moment it just feels so definitive - like proof that I don't measure up. I'm not sure how to break that cycle when the evidence feels so real to me.
therapist:
Your voice speeds up as you describe replaying that presentation—it’s clear how much this moment has stuck with you. It’s like your mind is on a loop, searching for every flaw as proof of not measuring up.  

But let’s pause here: when you compare yourself to others, are you comparing their highlights reel to your behind-the-scenes? That’s an unfair standard—one that’s bound to leave you feeling exhausted. What if we focused on what *did* go well in that presentation, however small?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I get what you're saying about comparing my behind-the-scenes to their highlights reel, but it’s hard not to. I keep thinking about how I stumbled over my words and how others seemed so polished. Even if something went well, it feels overshadowed by what went wrong. Focusing on the positives feels like I’m just sugarcoating it.
therapist:
Your voice softens when you talk about the positives feeling like sugarcoating—it sounds like you're wrestling with a deep skepticism that anything could outweigh the missteps. That hesitation makes sense when the criticism feels so much louder than the praise.  

What if we tried something different? Instead of forcing positivity, could we just notice the facts—like "I stumbled twice, *and* I covered all my key points"? No sugarcoating, just balance.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying about balancing the facts, but it’s hard for me to see it that way. When I stumble, it feels like it cancels out everything else I did right. It’s like my brain latches onto the mistakes and amplifies them, and the good stuff just fades into the background. I’m not sure if just noticing both sides will really change how I feel.
therapist:
Your voice quickens as you describe how mistakes seem to overshadow everything else—it’s clear how much weight you’re giving to those moments. That sense of cancellation feels so real, like the good stuff just disappears into the background.  

It’s understandable that simply noticing both sides might not feel like enough right now—it’s a shift that takes practice. What if we explored why those mistakes feel so defining? What story does your mind tell you when they happen?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
It’s like when I make a mistake, it’s all I can focus on, and it feels like it erases everything else I’ve done well. My mind tells me that I’m failing, that I’ll never get it right, and that people will notice and think less of me. It’s hard to even imagine that the good stuff still matters when that happens.  

I guess exploring why it feels so defining makes sense, but I’m not sure if it’ll change anything. It’s like the guilt and anxiety just take over, and I don’t know how to stop them from controlling how I see myself.
therapist:
Your voice rises and quickens as you describe this—it’s like the guilt and anxiety are racing ahead of you, leaving no room for anything else. That feeling of being controlled by them sounds exhausting, like you’re stuck in a loop where mistakes blot out everything else.  

When your mind says, "I’ll never get it right," it’s speaking with such certainty—but let’s challenge that. What if we slowed down and asked: *Has there ever been a time when a mistake didn’t erase the good?* Even a small example could help us find a crack in that pattern.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client:
I know what you're saying makes logical sense, but it's so hard to believe in the moment. When I make a mistake at work, it feels like that one error cancels out all the good things I've done for weeks. 

I can think of small examples where mistakes didn't ruin everything, like when I spilled coffee at a meeting last month and people just laughed it off. But those situations feel different - less important somehow. The bigger mistakes just haunt me.
therapist:
I hear how rushed and tense your voice gets when you talk about the bigger mistakes—it’s like they loom so large that even the examples of smaller slip-ups feel irrelevant by comparison. That divide makes sense when the stakes *feel* higher, but let’s gently question: What makes the bigger mistakes "haunt" you more? Is it the mistake itself, or the story you tell yourself about what it means?  

Even recalling that coffee spill is a start—it shows your mind *can* hold space for lighter moments. What if we explored what made that situation feel different? The laughter from others, maybe? Sometimes the gap between how we judge ourselves and how others see us is wider than we realize.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know, the coffee spill just felt...small, you know? Like it didn't define me as a person. But when I messed up that client presentation last month, it's like my brain keeps replaying it on loop. I guess the difference is that one felt like it revealed some deep flaw in me - like I'm incompetent and everyone can see it now. 

But even as I say that, part of me wonders if I'm being too hard on myself. My boss actually said it wasn't that bad, but I can't seem to believe her. Why does my brain latch onto the negative so much?
therapist:
Your voice speeds up and pitches higher as you describe this—it’s like your brain is stuck in overdrive, replaying that presentation while dismissing your boss’s reassurance. That disconnect between what she said and what you *feel* is so telling—it’s as if the fear of being "exposed" as incompetent drowns out everything else.  

You’re naming something powerful here: the difference between a small mistake and one that *feels* like it defines you. What if we got curious about why this presentation became proof of a "flaw"? Could it be that your standards for yourself are harsher than what you’d expect from anyone else?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
Yeah, I guess my standards are pretty harsh. But isn't that how you're supposed to be? If I don't hold myself to really high expectations, I'll just start slacking off completely. That presentation really was bad - my boss might say it was fine, but I *know* I stumbled over the numbers and lost my train of thought twice. 

It's just...when stuff like that happens, it feels like confirmation that I'm not as capable as everyone thinks. Like eventually they'll all see through me.
therapist:
Your voice drops quieter as you describe this—it’s like part of you is bracing for being "found out," even while another part recognizes these standards might be too harsh. That fear of slipping up and revealing some hidden inadequacy sounds so heavy to carry.  

You mention high expectations keep you from slacking—but what if we explored whether they might also be keeping you stuck in this cycle of dread? When you say, "I *know* it was bad," it’s with such certainty—yet your boss saw it differently. Could there be room for both truths: that you *did* stumble, *and* that it doesn’t define your capability?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client:
I get what you're saying about my standards being too harsh, but it's hard to accept that. When my boss said it wasn't a big deal, part of me thinks he was just being nice because he feels bad for me. The other part knows I'm probably overreacting, but the dread still feels so real. 

It's exhausting constantly worrying that people will realize I'm not as competent as they think. Even small mistakes make me feel like I've been "found out" like you said. Logically I know perfection is impossible, but my brain won't let me believe that applies to me.
therapist:
Your voice tightens and speeds up as you talk about being "found out"—it’s like you’re caught between logic and a deep, visceral fear that any misstep will unravel everything. That exhaustion comes through so clearly—it sounds like you’re constantly bracing for judgment, even when others offer kindness.  

What if we tried something? Let’s name that dread as it shows up: "Ah, there’s that old story again—the one where a mistake means I’m a fraud." Just noticing it, without fighting it, might help create a little space between you and that fear. Does that feel possible, even just a tiny bit?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
